configuration that no longer parses or a watched path that disappears, is reported, and the watch
goes on until it is fixed. A file counts as changed when its size, modification time, or (on Unix)
inode or status-change time changes, so a replacement that keeps the modification time is seen
too; a file stamped within the last two seconds is also compared by content, for file systems
whose timestamps are coarse.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/

# Coding Agents

heki's output is designed to be acted on by people and by coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
Cursor, and similar): every diagnostic says what was proven, where the evidence is, and what
blocks a fix.

## Use the CLI in the agent's loop

Ask the agent to run heki after editing and to read the JSON output:

```console
$ heki check --output-format json
```

Each diagnostic has:

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `path`, `line`, `column`, `span` | location (byte span in the file) |
| `rule_code`, `rule_slug`, `severity`, `message` | the finding |
| `qualname`, `target` | the function and the object involved |
| `related` | every hop of the call chain behind the finding |
| `evidence` | what was established (for `OPT` rules: the proof obligations) |
| `blocker` | the obligation that blocks an automatic fix, if any |
| `fix` | byte-span edits for proven-safe rewrites |

`heki rule <CODE>` prints a rule's documentation (what it does, why it matters, what to do
instead), which is a good prompt for the fix.

A typical instruction for the agent:

> After changing Python files, run `heki check --output-format json`. For each diagnostic,
> read `heki rule <rule_code>`, follow `related` to the root cause, and fix it there. Apply
> `heki check --fix` for the safe rewrites. Never silence a diagnostic with `# heki: ignore`
> unless the rule's documentation describes the case as intended.

## Use the LSP server

Agents that talk LSP (for example through an editor or an MCP bridge) can start
`heki server` and use diagnostics, related information, and code actions directly, as editors
do. See [Editors (LSP)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/).

## Documentation for models

The documentation is published in [llms.txt](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt) form, an index of every page with a
one-line description, and [llms-full.txt](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms-full.txt) with the full text of every page
including all rules.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/development/

# Development

## Build and test

```console
$ cargo build
$ cargo test --workspace
$ cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
```

The tests are end to end first: they run the real `heki` binary and the real LSP server
(`heki server --stdio`) on small projects. The `--fix` tests run the original and the rewritten
programs on CPython and require identical output; they use `python3.15`, or the interpreter in
`HEKI_TEST_PYTHON`.

Every line is covered except three that cannot run (the `_ => {}` arms for assignment,
augmented-assignment and `del` targets in `crates/heki_ir/src/builder.rs`, which the parser
rejects); CI fails on any other uncovered line:

```console
$ cargo llvm-cov --workspace --show-missing-lines --fail-uncovered-lines 3
```

The summary table counts the unit-test build and the normal build of a function separately and
keeps the better one, and it counts a closure that never runs as missed. Cover each function
completely from one side: end to end for analysis code, unit tests only for small guard functions.

## Checks against CPython

```console
$ cargo build
$ python3 tests/symtable_verify/verify_symtable.py --heki target/debug/heki tests/symtable_verify/fixtures/ tests/corpus/
$ python3 tests/sentinel/verify_soundness_kb.py
$ python3 tests/difftest/counterexamples.py
```

- `verify_symtable.py` compares heki's scope analysis with CPython's `symtable` (3.11 – 3.15):
  the scope tree (kind, name, definition line, parent), bindings, parameters, `global` /
  `nonlocal` declarations, and every read. Every target must exist and every file must parse on
  the running CPython, except fixtures marked for a newer one in their name (`312_315`,
  `313_315`, `_314`, `pep810`); a run that compares no file fails.
- `verify_soundness_kb.py` checks every claim of the Layer 1 knowledge base
  (`kb/soundness/builtins.toml`) on the running interpreter.
- `counterexamples.py` shows that the naive rewrites heki refuses really change behavior.

## Memory

```console
$ cargo build --release
$ python3 scripts/check_memory.py --heki target/release/heki
```

CI fails when the peak memory of `heki check` (with and without an ownership contract) or of
the `--watch` engine on a generated project exceeds its budget in the script (the lowest of three runs: the resident set size on Linux, the
physical footprint on macOS, each platform with its own budgets). The project is shaped after what dominates heki's memory on
real code bases: typed field writes reached through long chains of private helpers (with an
ownership contract, every caller keeps the write sites they hand over, with their chains), effect chains below `async def` entry points, and many
modules and classes (every file's check reads the project's declarations). When a budget is
exceeded, find what grew before raising it: `/usr/bin/time -l` (macOS) or `-v` (Linux) gives the
peak of a run, and a counting global allocator in a scratch build gives the live bytes per phase.

## Documentation

```console
$ cargo build --release
$ python scripts/build_docs.py --heki target/release/heki   # rules and CLI reference pages
$ python scripts/build_llms_txt.py                          # llms.txt / llms-full.txt
$ uvx --from "zensical==0.1.2" zensical serve
```

Rule documentation lives in `crates/heki_rules/rule-docs/<CODE>.md`; `heki rule <CODE>` prints it
and the generator copies it into `docs/rules/`. CI fails when the generated pages are stale.
The Docs workflow deploys the site to Cloudflare Pages (heki.koxudaxi.dev) once a published
release is on PyPI (the newest release only), or when it is run by hand on `main`, so the site
documents the released version;
only the `docs-production` environment holds that deployment's token. A pull request from this
repository gets a preview deployment in a separate Cloudflare account (project `heki-preview`).

## Architecture

The workspace is split by responsibility (`crates/`):

| Crate | Role |
| ----- | ---- |
| `heki_ast` | the only crate that depends on the parser (`ruff_python_parser`, pinned) |
| `heki_semantic` | scopes and bindings, checked against CPython's `symtable` |
| `heki_ir` | SSA control-flow-graph IR with explicit exception edges and loop information |
| `heki_kb` | the knowledge bases: Layer 1 (builtins semantics for the soundness lane) and Layer 2 (ecosystem effects) |
| `heki_effect` | call graph, per-function effect summaries, incremental project index |
| `heki_soundness` | the alias analysis and proof obligations behind `OPT` rewrites (never depends on `heki_effect`, never reads annotations) |
| `heki_rules` | the rules, rule selection, project discovery |
| `heki_diagnostics` | output formats, inline suppressions, Ratchet baselines, fix application |
| `heki_profile` | offline profile dumps |
| `heki_lsp` | the incremental LSP server and the `--watch` engine |
| `heki` | the command-line interface |

The internal design docs are in the repository:
[`ARCHITECTURE.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md) (the design),
[`docs/ANALYSIS_AND_KB_SPEC.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/ANALYSIS_AND_KB_SPEC.md)
(the analyses and knowledge bases), and
[`docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md)
(the decisions). [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/AGENTS.md) lists the
invariants every change must keep and the checks to run.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/

# async-blocking-call (EFF101)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Direct or indirect blocking network/DB/subprocess/sleep call reachable from `async def`.

## What it does
Checks `async def` functions that reach a blocking call on the event loop, directly or through
synchronous helpers: network I/O (`requests`, `httpx.Client`, `urllib`), database drivers
(`sqlite3`, `psycopg`, `pymongo`, ...; the fetches of a named, server-side psycopg cursor
`conn.cursor("name")` too), subprocesses waiting for completion, `time.sleep`, and
waits on other threads (acquiring a `threading` lock, `Event.wait()`, `Thread.join()`,
`queue.Queue.get()` / `put()`, `Future.result()`, `concurrent.futures.wait()`; a zero timeout or
`blocking=False` / `block=False` returns at once and is not reported, also when a helper passes
on its own flag parameter and its caller passes `False`: `close(wait=False)` over
`shutdown(wait=wait)`). A function SQLAlchemy's
`AsyncSession.run_sync(fn)` / `AsyncConnection.run_sync(fn)` runs is called on the event loop:
its database I/O through the session or connection it receives is awaited for it, its other
blocking calls are reported. Where an argument decides what a library call does, a literal
one is followed: `pd.read_csv("https://...")` downloads the file.

Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute of a project class runs its
getter, so the read counts as a call of the getter (`self.client` whose getter opens a
connection). A property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed.

Calling a generator function only creates the generator; its body runs where the generator is
iterated: a `for` loop or comprehension over it, unpacking it, `yield from` it, a call that
consumes it (`list(...)`, `sorted(...)`, `"".join(...)`, `items.extend(...)`, ...), a lazy wrapper
iterated there (`enumerate(...)`, `zip(...)`, `itertools.islice(...)`, ...), or a project
function iterating the parameter it is handed. A generator returned by a plain function runs
where its caller iterates it. `next(gen)` runs the body only up to its first `yield`, which heki
does not separate from the rest, so it is not followed.

A call whose arguments switch off the callee's branch with the blocking call is not followed
into it: `load(name, cache=False)` does not reach the request under `if cache:`. This covers
constant arguments and the literal defaults of omitted ones (`False`, `None`, `0`, `""`, empty
displays), and tests the caller has already made on the same value: a call made only when
`isinstance(self._input, PathLike)` is false does not reach the callee's branch for
`isinstance(self._input, PathLike)`. A generator's branches are decided at the call that
creates it. Lazy initialization does not relax this rule: a connection opened once still
blocks the event loop that once.

The rule reports the boundary: the call (or property read, or iteration) inside the `async def`
that leads to the blocking operation, with the call chain as related information. Several
boundaries reaching the same blocking call are shown as one report with a count once more than
ten of them are shown (in the editor, per file). Inline suppressions and Ratchet baselines see
every boundary: suppressing the first one leaves the others reported, and a baseline counts each.

It does not report:

- calls offloaded to a thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`,
  `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, `run_in_threadpool`, `asgiref`'s `sync_to_async`,
  `asyncer.asyncify`, and project wrappers that forward their callable to them; what the
  offloaded function does besides blocking still counts where it is called, such as its
  queries in a loop for `EFF103`);
- functions decorated to run on a thread: `@sync_to_async` (also as a factory,
  `@sync_to_async(thread_sensitive=False)`), `channels`' `@database_sync_to_async`, `@asyncify`,
  and any decorator declared with `offloads-blocking-arg = 0`. `@d def f` is `f = d(f)`, so
  calling `f` calls `d(f)`; other decorators (`functools.wraps` wrappers) are followed;
- generators that leave the `async def` without being iterated there: returned, stored, or
  handed to a call that is not a consuming one, such as `StreamingResponse(rows())` or
  `iterate_in_threadpool(rows())` (whatever iterates them later, often a thread pool, is not
  analyzed);
- `async` APIs, also where they are not awaited directly (`async with`, `asyncio.gather`,
  `asyncio.wait_for`): `httpx.AsyncClient`, `aiohttp`, `redis.asyncio`, SQLAlchemy's
  `AsyncSession`, psycopg's `AsyncConnection`, pymongo's `AsyncMongoClient`, ...;
- clients that connect on first use (`redis.Redis(...)`, `pymongo.MongoClient(...)`, except
  that a `mongodb+srv://` URI literal is resolved in the constructor unless `connect=False`,
  `pymysql.connect(..., defer_connect=True)`, `sqlalchemy.create_engine(...)`) and calls that
  only build an object (`Redis.pipeline()`, a
  lazy Django `QuerySet.filter(...)`): the call that does the I/O is the one reported;
- spawning a process without waiting (`subprocess.Popen(...)`);
- private coroutine functions that only run through a synchronous driver without an event loop
  (`.send(None)`, a `run_sync` function); `asyncio.run(...)` runs its coroutine on an event loop,
  where blocking stops the tasks it starts;
- CLI commands (`@click.command`, `@app.command`), ASGI lifespan handlers, and tests
  (`test_*` functions and files under `tests/`, see the option below).

## Why is this bad?
A blocking call inside a coroutine stops the whole event loop: every other request, timer, and
task waits until it returns.

## Example
```python
import time


def load() -> bytes:
    time.sleep(1)
    return b""


async def handler() -> bytes:
    return load()  # EFF101: reaches `time.sleep`
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio


async def handler() -> bytes:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(load)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` (default `true`): skip test code.
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` declares project functions as blocking (`effects`), as offload
  wrappers (`offloads-blocking-arg`; with `0`, also an offloading decorator), or as async-safe
  (`async-safe`).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/

# async-blocking-fs (EFF105)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Opt-in · No automatic fix

Opt-in: blocking local filesystem I/O reachable from `async def`.

## What it does
Checks `async def` functions that reach blocking local filesystem I/O: `open(...)`,
`pathlib.Path.read_text` / `write_text` / `read_bytes` / `write_bytes` / `open`, `os.listdir`,
`os.scandir`, iterating `os.walk(...)`, `shutil` copies and removals, and the pandas file readers
(`pd.read_csv(path)`; one given a URL literal downloads it and is `EFF101`, one given an
`io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` buffer does no I/O). It follows the same boundary,
offload, and guard rules as `EFF101`, generators and offloading decorators included: `await
in_thread(self.open) if isinstance(self._input, PathLike) else self.open()` is not reported
when `open` only opens a file under `isinstance(self._input, PathLike)`.

This rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select EFF105` or `extend-select = ["EFF105"]`.
Selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.

## Why is this bad?
Local file I/O is usually fast, which is why it is opt-in, but on network file systems, large
files, or busy disks it blocks the event loop like any other blocking call.

## Example
```python
async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path) as f:  # EFF105
        return f.read()
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio
from pathlib import Path


async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(Path(path).read_text)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF105"]` enables the rule.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/

# cached-property-stale-mutation (MUT101)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache.

## What it does
Checks for methods that rebind or mutate an attribute that a `@functools.cached_property`
of the same class (or of a subclass) reads, without invalidating the cached value. A method the
class inherits from a project base class and does not override runs on its instances too, so it
is checked against the class's cached properties (reported in the base class).
A decorator is known by what its name is bound to in the module: an import alias counts
(`from functools import cached_property as cached`), a decorator the module defines itself does
not (a `def cache(fn)` of its own), and a name bound by neither counts by its spelling.

## Why is this bad?
A `cached_property` computes its value once and stores it in the instance `__dict__`. Once the
attribute it was computed from changes, the property keeps returning the old value until the
cache entry is deleted. The stale value is usually noticed far away from the write.

The rule follows `self.helper()` calls in both directions (a property that reads through a
helper, a method that writes through a helper) and the getters of the properties the cached
property reads (`self.key` where the `@property` `key` reads `self.name`), and reports the write
itself, once per property. A property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed.
It does not report:

- two-phase initialization: `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`,
  `__enter__`, `setup`, `_init_*` / `_configure_*` methods, and private helpers called from
  `__init__`;
- memo / cache dictionaries (`self._cache[key] = value`, `setdefault`, the
  `if key not in self._memo:` pattern): in-place changes of an attribute with a `cache` or
  `memo` word in its name; rebinding it (`self.cache_size = n`) and names such as
  `memory_limit` are no memo operation;
- constant dictionary keys the property never reads (`self.params["proxy"]` while the property
  reads `self.params["outtmpl"]`);
- writes after which every path invalidates the property (`del self.prop`,
  `self.__dict__.pop("prop", None)`, a `self` method that does), or before which every path
  already did and nothing read it since; an invalidation under a condition, such as
  `if clear:`, leaves the other path stale and is reported;
- private helpers whose every caller invalidates the property;
- changes made in place (`clear()`, `append()`, item assignment) to an attribute whose object
  the cached value holds itself, when the getter reads it for nothing else: it returns
  `self.items`, or puts it as itself into a display or a container it returns
  (`{"items": self.items}`, `ctx["k"] = (x, self.items)`). The cached value sees those changes;
  rebinding the attribute (`self.items = []`) is still reported. A getter that also computes
  from it (`len(self.items)`), copies it (`list(self.items)`, `(*self.items,)`), reads it through
  a `self` method or property, or hands `self` to other code is reported as before.

## Example
```python
from functools import cached_property


class Settings:
    def __init__(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw

    @cached_property
    def keys(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return tuple(self.raw)

    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw  # `self.keys` still returns the old keys
```

Use instead:
```python
    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw
        self.__dict__.pop("keys", None)  # or `del self.keys` when it was computed
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to invalidate, recompute, or make the attribute read-only is a design
decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/

# call-owner-violation (MUT204)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`.

## What it does
Checks calls of functions and methods, and constructions of classes, that a
`[[tool.heki.call-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of allowed callers: the call side of
`MUT201` (who may write) and `MUT203` (who may read). A call is reported when it happens outside
the allowed callers and resolves to a target:

- a method called on an instance of the target's class or of a subclass, including an override of
  the method in a subclass (`data_type.replace_reference(ref)`);
- the same method through a bound-method alias (`replace = data_type.replace_reference`, then
  `replace(ref)`) or `getattr(data_type, "replace_reference")(...)` with a constant name;
- a module-level function (`pkg.util.reset_cache()`);
- a class: constructing it or a subclass (`FinalFacts(...)`, `pkg.facts.FinalFacts(...)`,
  `cls(...)` in a class method), also for a dataclass or another class without an `__init__` of
  its own.

A call is reported only when every function it may call is a target: when the receiver's class
hierarchy also offers a method that is no target (a receiver typed with a base class whose own
`replace_reference` is not guarded), the call is not reported. The functions it may call can be
targets of different entries of one contract: with `A.reset` and `B.reset` both listed, `obj.reset()`
on `obj: Base`, whose subclasses `A` and `B` implement `reset`, is one report for
`A.reset|B.reset`. A call on a receiver whose class heki does not know (an unannotated
parameter, `Any`) is not seen.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with project
callers hands its calls to its callers: the call is reported at the call sites of the first
non-private callers, with the chain of calls down to the call as related information. A call runs
where the body holding it runs, as for `MUT201`: a generator's calls where it is iterated (a
generator an allowed caller creates and returns calls outside it when its caller iterates it), a
coroutine's where it is awaited. Not reported either:

- a function that only runs inside allowed callers: it has project callers, and every path of
  callers above it starts in an allowed caller, an exempt method, or a class's own
  initialization (as for `MUT201`);
- a class's own initialization: an initializer (`__init__`, `__post_init__`, ...) of a class of
  the target's family calling a guarded method on its own `self`;
- a target calling a target of the same contract (`remove_reference` calling
  `self.replace_reference(None)`, an override calling `super().replace_reference(...)`): the
  guarded operation is checked where it is called, so what it does inside is part of it.

## Why is this bad?
Some operations keep invariants only when one component runs them: a store that updates its
indexes after redirecting a reference, a factory that builds a sealed object exactly once. A
direct call from elsewhere skips the bookkeeping, and nothing fails until an input exercises the
stale state. A linter cannot tell `data_type.replace_reference(ref)` from `text.replace("a", "b")`
without the receiver's class, and an import rule cannot forbid a method of an object the caller
legitimately imports. The contract states the ownership once in configuration.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference", "FinalFacts"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.store.GenerationStore.*"]
message = "use a GenerationStore operation instead"
```

```python
# pkg/store.py
class GenerationStore:
    def replace_data_type_ref(self, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
        data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # allowed caller


def swap(data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # MUT204: outside `pkg.store.GenerationStore.*`


def rename(text: str) -> str:
    return text.replace("a", "b")  # not reported: a `str`, not a `DataType`
```

Use instead:
```python
def swap(store: GenerationStore, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    store.replace_data_type_ref(data_type, ref)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: functions, methods, or classes, as dotted names or globs matched against the fully
    qualified name and any dotted suffix (`DataType.replace_reference`, `pkg.util.reset_cache`,
    `FinalFacts`, `Parser._*`). A `Class.method` target covers the method's overrides in
    subclasses; a class target covers constructing the class and its subclasses.
  - `allowed-callers`: functions allowed to call the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname (`pkg.store.*`).
  - `forbidden-callers`: when set, only calls by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-callers`); `allowed-callers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A
    call is in scope when the reporting function or one of the private helpers it hands the call
    through is forbidden (`forbidden-callers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not call
    the targets).
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to call the targets (`__deepcopy__`); a plain name matches
    any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched like
    `allowed-callers`.
  - `message`: appended to every message of the contract.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/

# effect-boundary-violation (EFF201)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Reaching a forbidden effect (directly or through calls) from a declared `effect-boundaries` scope.

## What it does
Checks the functions of a declared effect boundary (`[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]`): they
must not reach a forbidden effect, directly or through the functions they call. Reading a
`@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute of a project class calls its getter; a
property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed, so its setter's writes never
count for a read.

- `scopes` select the checked functions. A pattern names a module (`pkg.domain`,
  `pkg.domain.*`), a class (`pkg.Renderer`), or a function (`*.render`); every function defined
  inside a matched name is in scope, nested functions included. Patterns are matched against
  the function's qualified name, its qualname, and every dotted prefix of them, so `render` also
  selects a module named `render`.
- `forbid` lists the forbidden effects:
  - `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`, `blocking-sync`,
    `sleep`, or `blocking` for all six: blocking calls of the ecosystem knowledge base
    (`requests.get`, `sqlite3`, `open`, `subprocess.run`, `time.sleep`, ...);
  - `writes-targets`: writes to the `Class.attr` entries of `write-targets` (and their
    subclasses), or to one entry of the container an attribute holds (`Class.attr["key"]`), in
    every form `MUT201` follows, through the receivers whose class `MUT201` sees (the items of
    annotated containers included); a class's own initialization is no write (constructing a
    fresh object runs its `__init__`), and neither is a write that constructs the object it
    writes (`fresh-objects = "allow"`, the default; a write the reached function makes to an
    object it allocated), as for `MUT201`;
  - `reads-targets`: reads of the `Class.attr` entries of `read-targets` (and their
    subclasses), in every form `MUT203` follows (`obj.attr`, `getattr(obj, "attr")`,
    `obj.__dict__["attr"]`, a property getter that reads it); an initializer reading its own
    instance is no read;
  - `calls`: calls of the `call-targets` entries, matched as the targets of `MUT204`: a function,
    a method (with its overrides in subclasses, through bound-method aliases and `getattr` with a
    constant name), or a class (constructing it); a call is one only when every function it may
    call is a target;
  - `mutates-params`: mutating a parameter, its attributes, or its contents. For a method,
    parameter 0 is `self`, so a method writing `self.x` mutates a parameter.
- `write-universe` with `allow-writes` states the writes a scope may make positively: a reached
  write of a `write-universe` entry that no `allow-writes` entry names is reported, in every form
  `writes-targets` follows. `allow-writes` also exempts writes from `write-targets` in the same
  boundary. Without `allow-writes`, the boundary allows no write of the universe.

Each scope function is searched breadth first over the project call graph, so the reported
chain is a shortest one. The search does not enter:

- `allowed-callees` (project functions or ecosystem symbols, matched like `scopes`): their
  effects are allowed, also when a helper hands them a field it was given
  (`helper(model.fields)` writes nothing when `helper` only passes `fields` to an allowed
  callee that changes it);
- other functions of the scopes: each reports its own violations, so a violation is reported
  once, at the boundary, not again by every scope function above it;
- `async def` functions called without `await` (calling one only creates a coroutine), and
  generators that are not iterated (calling a generator function only creates the generator;
  its body is searched where it is iterated, as for `EFF101`, and a generator a function
  returns where the object it returns is iterated);
- functions an offloading decorator or API runs on another thread (`@sync_to_async`,
  `asyncio.to_thread(f)`, ...).

A violation is reported once per scope function and forbidden effect (or write, read, or call
target; a `write-universe` write once per written `Class.attr`), at the call in the scope
function that starts the shortest chain (or at the blocking call, write, read, or call itself),
with the chain as related information; `mutates-params` is reported at the function's
definition. The report counts every distinct site of that kind the scope function reaches
(`sites` in JSON; for `mutates-params`, every change of a parameter, in the body making it), so
a Ratchet baseline sees a second blocking call, write, or parameter change below a recorded
report.

`allow-writes` is only as precise as heki's view of which object each write changes. A write
heki cannot tell apart from a write of the pass's input is reported: state that a property
getter writes while rendering, or a store operation whose writes depend on its arguments. A
write that constructs the object it writes is not (`fresh-objects = "allow"`). Treat its
reports as candidates to review, or narrow the universe, rather than gating on it.

## Why is this bad?
Some parts of a code base promise to be pure: rendering a model must not mutate it, domain code
must not do network I/O, a hot path must not sleep. The promise usually breaks several calls
away from the function that makes it, where a reviewer does not look. The boundary states it
once in configuration and checks every path.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pure-render"
scopes = ["*.render"]
forbid = ["blocking", "writes-targets"]
write-targets = ["DataModel.fields"]
allowed-callees = ["pkg.cache.*"]
message = "render entry points must not mutate model state"
```

```python
import requests


def get_json(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url).json()


class Model:
    def render(self) -> str:
        data = get_json("https://example.com")  # EFF201: reaches `requests.get`
        return str(data)
```

Use instead:
```python
class Model:
    def render(self, data: dict) -> str:
        return str(data)  # the caller fetches `data` before rendering
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]`:
  - `name`: the boundary name, used in messages and in the diagnostic target
    (`pure-render:blocking_net`, `pure-render:DataModel.fields` for a write,
    `pure-render:reads:DataModel.fields`, `pure-render:calls:GenerationStore.*`,
    `pure-render:mutates-params`), so a read and a write of one field are two reports.
  - `scopes`: modules, classes, or functions (dotted names or globs).
  - `forbid`: `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`,
    `blocking-sync`, `sleep`, `blocking`, `mutates-params`, `writes-targets`, `reads-targets`,
    `calls`.
  - `write-targets`: `Class.attr` entries for `writes-targets` (required with it).
  - `read-targets`: `Class.attr` entries for `reads-targets` (required with it).
  - `call-targets`: functions, methods, or classes for `calls` (required with it), as for the
    `targets` of `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`.
  - `write-universe`: `Class.attr` entries whose reached writes are reported unless
    `allow-writes` names them; the diagnostic target is the entry, with a glob attribute replaced
    by the written one (`pass:DataModel.fields` for `DataModel.*`).
  - `allow-writes`: `Class.attr` writes the boundary allows (needs `write-universe`).
  - `fresh-objects`: `"allow"` (default) or `"report"`: whether writes that construct the object
    they write count, as for `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]`.
  - `allowed-callees`: functions, classes, modules, or ecosystem symbols whose effects are
    allowed.
  - `message`: appended to every message of the boundary.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/

# hash-attr-mutation (MUT107)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Mutating an attribute read by `__hash__` after initialization (stored `set` / `dict` entries become unreachable).

## What it does
Checks methods that rebind or mutate an attribute that the class's `__hash__` reads (directly,
through a `self.helper()` call, or through the getter of a property it reads, such as
`hash(self.key)` where the `@property` `key` reads `self.name`), when the class, one of its
subclasses, or a base-class method it inherits without overriding changes the attribute after
initialization. A property that also defines a setter
or deleter is not followed.

The rule reports the write itself, once per method and attribute. It does not report:

- initialization: `__new__`, `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`,
  `__enter__`, `setup`, `_init_*` / `_configure_*` methods, and the private helpers they call
  (`self.__setstate(state)` on the instance `__new__` allocates included); class attributes
  that `__init_subclass__` sets;
- lazy initialization: a write under a `None` / falsy check of the same attribute
  (`if self._key is None: self._key = ...`, `if not self._parts: ...`);
- memo / cache dictionaries (`self._cache[key] = value`, `setdefault`, the
  `if key not in self._memo:` pattern): in-place changes of an attribute with a `cache` or
  `memo` word in its name; rebinding it (`self.cache_size = n`) and names such as
  `memory_limit` are no memo operation;
- constant dictionary keys `__hash__` never reads (`self.meta["note"]` while `__hash__` reads
  `self.meta["id"]`);
- the hash's own cache: an attribute the hash computation writes itself (`self._hash = ...`
  in `__hash__` or a `self.helper()` it calls), which other methods reset, and a stored hash
  value (`self._hash`, `self._hashcode`) that a deserialization hook recomputes.

## Why is this bad?
A `set` or a `dict` files an object under the hash it had when it was added. Once an attribute
the hash is computed from changes, lookups compute a different hash and look in the wrong
place: `obj in seen` is `False` for an object that is in `seen`, a `dict` holds a key no
lookup finds, and the object can be added a second time.

## Example
```python
class Tag:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        return isinstance(other, Tag) and other.name == self.name

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash(self.name)

    def rename(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name  # a `Tag` in a set can no longer be found
```

Use instead:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tag:
    name: str


def rename(tag: Tag, name: str) -> Tag:
    return replace(tag, name=name)  # a new object, hashed when it is stored
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to make the object immutable, hash only fields that never change,
or remove the object from its containers before changing it is a design decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/immutable-quadratic-concat/

# immutable-quadratic-concat (OPT103)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Size-dependent immutable quadratic accumulation (`bytes`/`tuple`/attr `str`).

## What it does
Checks quadratic accumulation of immutable values in a loop:

- `acc = acc + chunk` / `acc += chunk` where `acc` is a `bytes` or `tuple`;
- `self.text += piece` on an attribute that the class's methods in the module (or, for another
  receiver, the function) only ever assign a string, bytes, or tuple literal of the pieces'
  kind (`self.text = ""`): `self.values += (i,)` extends a list in place.

Local `str` accumulation is not reported: CPython already appends in place when the string has
no other reference. Neither are:

- an accumulator the loop's own test caps at a small constant (`while len(buf) < 10`, also
  as one `and` operand or with a module constant: at most 4096), whatever the input;
- `obj.attr += x` where `obj` is a different object in every iteration (the loop element, or
  an object created in the iteration): each attribute gets one piece.

## Why is this bad?
Each concatenation copies everything accumulated so far.

## Example
```python
def encode(parts: list[bytes]) -> bytes:
    out = b""
    for p in parts:
        out = out + p
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def encode(parts: list[bytes]) -> bytes:
    return b"".join(parts)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix (the rewrite needs a buffer before the loop and a join after it). The
diagnostic still lists the proof obligations: the accumulator must not be read inside the loop
or by an exception handler, and its intermediate values must not escape.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/

# iterator-double-consumption (MUT106)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Opt-in · No automatic fix

Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items).

## What it does
Checks for a single-pass iterator or generator that is consumed a second time. Once an
iterator is exhausted, every further pass over it sees no items, silently.

Single-pass values are:

- generator expressions (`(x for x in xs)`);
- `iter`, `zip`, `map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `reversed`, `heapq.merge`, and the single-pass
  `itertools` functions (`chain`, `islice`, `starmap`, `takewhile`, `dropwhile`, `filterfalse`,
  `compress`, `accumulate`, `groupby`, `pairwise`, `batched`, `zip_longest`, `product`,
  `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement`), resolved through imports
  so a shadowed name is never matched;
- calls of project generator functions (from any module);
- parameters and locals annotated `Iterator`, `Generator`, `AsyncIterator`, or
  `AsyncGenerator` (`typing` or `collections.abc`; `Iterable`, `Sequence`, and `Collection`
  may be re-iterable and are not tracked).

A value is consumed by a `for` loop or comprehension over it, unpacking (`a, *rest = it`),
`yield from`, a call that materializes it (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `frozenset`, `dict`, `bytes`,
`bytearray`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`, `str.join`, `bytes.join`,
`dict.fromkeys`, `list.extend`, `set.update` / `union` / `intersection` / `difference`,
`dict.update`, `collections.deque` / `Counter` / `OrderedDict` / `defaultdict`,
`heapq.nlargest` / `nsmallest`, `functools.reduce`, `math.prod` / `fsum`), a wrapper that is
itself consumed (`enumerate(it)`, `map(f, it)`, `chain(it, other)`, `heapq.merge(it, other)`,
`zip(it, it)`, a generator expression over it, ...), or a project function that iterates the
parameter it is passed to exhaustion (for a method, every implementation the call may run must;
an `@abstractmethod` never runs). `next(it)` and `len` are not consumptions, and neither are
`zip` / `map` over several iterables, `islice`, or `takewhile`: they stop at the shortest one or
early (`zip(range(n), it)` takes `n` items). The same table decides where a generator's body
runs for the effect and contract rules.

The rule reports the second pass when the first one runs to exhaustion and the second is
reachable from it, without rebinding the variable in between. It also reports a value created
outside a loop and consumed to exhaustion inside it: the next iteration sees nothing.

It does not report:

- a first pass that may stop early: a `for` loop with `break`, `return`, or `raise` inside
  (`it = iter(lines)`, then `for line in it: ... break`, then `for line in it:` is the
  idiomatic way to resume), and `any(it)` / `all(it)`, which stop at the first item that decides
  the result (they still run a generator's body where they are called);
- passes on exclusive branches (`if c: list(it) else: sorted(it)`);
- a variable rebound to a fresh iterator in between;
- `itertools.tee` results, `repeat`, `cycle`, and `count`;
- loops that run at most once (`for _ in range(1)`), and a consumption followed by leaving the
  loop (`data = list(it)` then `break`);
- consuming the rest of an iterator inside a loop over that iterator itself.

## Why is this bad?
The second pass silently gets an empty iterator: totals become zero, a second report is empty,
and a retry processes nothing. Nothing fails, so the bug is noticed far away from its cause.

## Example
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = (line.strip() for line in lines)
    count = sum(1 for _ in rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]  # MUT106: `rows` was consumed by `sum`
    return count, kept
```

Use instead:
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = [line.strip() for line in lines]  # a list can be iterated any number of times
    count = len(rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]
    return count, kept
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT106"]` (or `--extend-select MUT106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/

# list-front-insert (OPT121)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that insert at the front of a list, `q.insert(0, v)`, and suggests a
`collections.deque` with `appendleft(v)`.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions. A list rebuilt in every iteration of the loop is not reported: its front insert
costs no more than building it.

## Why is this bad?
Inserting at the front shifts every element, so building a list this way is quadratic.

## Example
```python
def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in items:
        out.insert(0, i)
    return list(out)
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = collections.deque()
    for i in items:
        out.appendleft(i)
    return list(out)
```

## Fix safety
The same obligations as `OPT120`, and the same rewrite of annotations and imports.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/

# list-front-pop (OPT120)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that remove the first element of a list: `q.pop(0)`, `del q[0]`, and
`q = q[1:]`, and suggests a `collections.deque` with `popleft()`.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions. The rewrite changes the list's creation to `collections.deque(...)`, rewrites the
variable's `list[...]` annotation to `collections.deque[...]`, and adds `import collections`
when needed: in sorted position among the module's standard-library imports, or after the
docstring and `__future__` imports of a module without other imports.

Not reported: a small display that the loop only drains (`expected = [b"a", b""]` and
`expected.pop(0)` in the loop: it never holds more than its items), and a list rebuilt in every
iteration of the loop.

## Why is this bad?
Removing the first element shifts every remaining element, so a queue drained this way is
quadratic. `deque.popleft()` is constant time.

## Example
```python
def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = [start]
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = collections.deque([start])
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is created in the function, never leaves it (not returned,
stored, or passed to other code except read-only builtins such as `len`), and every use has a
`deque` equivalent: no sorting, no slicing, no indexes other than `0` and `-1`, no `==`
against lists. An annotation the rewrite cannot turn into a `deque` one (`Sequence[str]`, a
union) or another annotated declaration of the variable blocks the fix, so that a type checker
accepts the fixed file.

A `deque` iterator raises `RuntimeError` when the deque changes under it and is another type
than a list iterator: no iterator of the list may be live at a change, consumed by the changing
call (`q.extend(reversed(q))`), or used for more than its elements (`type(iter(q))`). `list(xs)`
of a value that is not a builtin container becomes `deque(list(xs))`, which keeps the length
query `list` makes; `list(**kw)` and `list(*args)` block the fix (`deque` reads a second
argument as `maxlen`). Only `q = q[1:]` is a front pop: `q[1:n]` and `q[1::2]` are not.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/

# list-quadratic-concat (OPT101)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Safe fix (`--fix`)

Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a list by building a new one every iteration, `x = x + [e]`, and
rewrites it to `x.append(e)` (`x.extend([...])` for several elements).

## Why is this bad?
`x + [e]` copies the whole list, so the loop is quadratic. `append` is amortized constant time
and is never slower, even for one iteration.

## Example
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out = out + [i * i]
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(i * i)
    return out
```

## Fix safety
The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` only when heki proves it safe:

- the list is an exact builtin `list` created in the function, not shared (not a parameter,
  not stored in another object, not captured by a closure, not passed to unknown code);
- no other reference to the old list is live after the statement: no alias, no `for` loop
  iterating it, no `iter(x)` or view;
- evaluating the right-hand side does not rebind or mutate the list;
- no exception handler can observe an older binding of another name aliasing it.

Otherwise the diagnostic explains which proof obligation blocks the fix, and nothing is
rewritten. A disproved candidate is not reported at all: `for v in x: x = x + [v]` terminates,
but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki says nothing there and never touches it. Type
annotations are never trusted.

The fix rewrites a plain `x = x + [...]` statement. For other shapes of the same update (a
parenthesized `x = (x + [i])` or `x = (x) + [i]`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`), the
diagnostic says that the rewrite is proven safe and leaves it to be made by hand.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/

# lock-or-tx-held-across-io (EFF106)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Opt-in · No automatic fix

Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction.

## What it does
Checks for an `await`, or a call reaching blocking network I/O (directly or through project
helpers, including the getter of a property read), while a `with` block holds a synchronous
lock or a database transaction.

The held resource must be type-certain:

- an instance of `threading.Lock`, `RLock`, `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`, or `Condition`,
  created in `__init__` (`self._lock = threading.Lock()`), at module level, locally, or given
  by an annotated parameter;
- a transaction started by `sqlalchemy.orm.Session.begin()` / `begin_nested()`,
  `Connection.begin()` / `begin_nested()`, `Engine.begin()`, `sqlmodel.Session.begin()`,
  `django.db.transaction.atomic()`, or `psycopg.Connection.transaction()`.

The rule reports the `await` or the call while the resource is certainly held (on every path),
with the call chain to the network I/O as related information. Leaving the `with` block
releases what that block acquired: a re-entrant lock entered again by a nested `with` stays held
until the outer block exits.

It does not report:

- `async with` and async locks (`asyncio.Lock`, `anyio.Lock`, ...);
- objects whose type is not known, or not a registered lock or transaction;
- work after the `with` block, and handlers reached only after the block exited;
- calls offloaded to a thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`, ...);
- database queries inside a transaction, local file I/O, or `time.sleep`;
- CLI commands, ASGI lifespan handlers, and tests, as for `EFF101`.

## Why is this bad?
A synchronous lock held across an `await` blocks every thread that wants it until the coroutine
resumes, and a second coroutine acquiring it on the event loop thread deadlocks the loop. Held
across a network request, the lock serializes every waiting thread behind that request. A
transaction held across a request or an `await` keeps its pooled connection checked out and its
row locks taken, which exhausts the pool under load.

## Example
```python
import asyncio
import threading


class Cache:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._data: dict[str, bytes] = {}

    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._data[key] = await fetch(key)  # EFF106
```

Use instead:
```python
    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        value = await fetch(key)
        with self._lock:  # hold the lock only for the update
            self._data[key] = value
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF106"]` (or `--extend-select EFF106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/

# loop-carried-concat (DATA101)

Family: Data Pipelines (DATA) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation.

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a DataFrame or array by re-concatenating it on every iteration:
`df = pd.concat([df, chunk])`, `arr = np.vstack([arr, row])`, `arr = np.append(arr, x)`, and
the other quadratic reallocations of the ecosystem knowledge base. Only loop-carried
accumulation is reported: the result feeds the next iteration and is computed from the previous
value, also when it grows on some iterations only. An update through a project function counts
when that function returns a reallocation of the argument carrying the previous value, directly
or through further helpers (`acc = grow(acc)` where `grow` returns `np.append(acc, x)`); a helper
that reallocates something else and returns its argument unchanged does not. One-off
concatenations inside a loop are not reported, also on a branch that leaves the variable
unchanged otherwise (`if step: x = np.append(edges, last)`), nor is writing into a buffer passed
as `out=` (`out = np.concatenate(([a], [b]), out=out)` reuses the same buffer): the previous
value must be among the data that is combined.

## Why is this bad?
Every concatenation copies everything accumulated so far, so the loop is quadratic in the total
size.

## Example
```python
import pandas as pd


def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    for chunk in chunks:
        df = pd.concat([df, chunk])  # DATA101
    return df
```

Use instead:
```python
def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.concat(chunks) if chunks else pd.DataFrame()  # `pd.concat([])` raises
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/

# loop-db-query (EFF103)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Explicit DB query / external RPC executed inside a loop (N+1).

## What it does
Checks loops that run a database query on every iteration (the "N+1 queries" problem):
`cursor.execute(...)`, `session.execute(...)` (awaited ones on async sessions and connections
too), the SQLAlchemy `Query` methods that run the query (`all`, `first`, `one`, `count`, ...)
and iterating a `Query` (`for row in session.query(User):` in an outer loop, a comprehension,
`list(query)`),
the Django `QuerySet` methods that run the query (`get`, `first`, `count`, ... and their `a*`
variants), `pymongo`, `redis`, and DynamoDB commands, `pandas.read_sql`, and project functions
that reach them, also when an offloading API runs them on a worker thread per item (`await
asyncio.to_thread(load, i)`, a function decorated with `@sync_to_async`), including the getter of a property read in the loop and a generator iterated in
the loop (its body runs where it is iterated, as for `EFF101`).

It does not report reading the rows of a statement already executed (`cursor.fetchone()`),
calls that only build a query (`session.query(User).filter(...)`, `QuerySet.filter(...)`,
`Redis.pipeline()`), the bulk APIs, which send many rows in one statement and are called per
batch by design (`QuerySet.bulk_create`, `in_bulk`, pymongo's `insert_many`, `bulk_write`), DDL
statements (a literal starting with `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, or `PRAGMA` run by a DB-API
`execute` / `executemany` / `executescript`, also inside a helper the loop calls), migration code
(`upgrade` / `downgrade` functions, files under `migrations/` or `alembic/`), the ORM packages'
own implementation, or loops whose size the code fixes when no data-sized loop is around them
(`for ident in enumerate((1, 2), 1)`, `zip(order, ["m1", "m2"])`, a name bound to a small
display; see `EFF102`).

As for `EFF102`, a query that only runs while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets
(`if self._columns is None: self._columns = cursor.execute(...)`), runs once per object and is
not reported when the loop does not construct the object; a call whose arguments switch off
the branch with the query (a constant, a literal default, a test the caller has made) is not
followed into it.

## Why is this bad?
One round trip per item makes the run time grow with the number of rows and with the network
latency to the database. A single batched query is usually orders of magnitude faster.

## Example
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for i in ids:
        cursor.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?", (i,))  # EFF103
        out.append(cursor.fetchone()[0])
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    if not ids:
        return []
    marks = ",".join("?" * len(ids))
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id IN ({marks})", ids)
    name_of = dict(cursor.fetchall())
    return [name_of[i] for i in ids]  # `KeyError` for an unknown ID (the loop: `TypeError`)
```

The query returns each matching row once and in no particular order, so the result is rebuilt
from the IDs: in their order, with repeated IDs repeated. A database caps the number of
parameters in one statement; split a long list of IDs into chunks.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/

# loop-invariant-container-rebuild (OPT130)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that rebuild the same container on every iteration just to test membership,
`e in set(keys)` (also `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `dict(...)`), and suggests building it once
before the loop.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions.

## Why is this bad?
The container is rebuilt from scratch on every iteration, which costs as much as the scan it
was meant to avoid.

## Example
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in set(keys):
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

Use instead:
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    keys_set = set(keys)
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in keys_set:
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the rebuilt expression is a builtin constructor without side effects,
every value it reads is bound outside the loop and not changed inside it, and building it before
the loop cannot raise even when the loop runs zero times (hashable builtin elements). The
container must be used by the membership test only: `(tmp := list(keys))` followed by
`tmp.clear()` would clear the one shared container. Calls with `*` arguments (`list(*args)`
passes the elements of `args`) and method calls with arguments are not hoisted.

Not reported when the loop runs a fixed small number of times, or when nothing is rebuilt:
`tuple(t)` of a tuple returns `t` itself.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/

# loop-linear-dedup (OPT111)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`.

## What it does
Checks the de-duplication idiom `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` inside a loop and suggests
keeping an auxiliary `set` next to the list.

Size-dependent: applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in profiled hot
functions.

## Why is this bad?
The membership test scans the list, so de-duplicating `n` items costs `n²` comparisons.

## Example
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.append(v)
    return seen
```

Use instead:
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    seen_set = set()
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen_set:
            seen.append(v)
            seen_set.add(v)
    return seen
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is an exact builtin list owned by the function, the paired
`append` is its only change inside the loop (a removal would make the set stale), no other live
reference could change it, and every element and probe is a hashable builtin scalar.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/

# loop-linear-list-lookup (OPT112)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans).

## What it does
Checks `list.index()`, `list.remove()`, and `list.count()` calls that run on every iteration
of a loop, on a list that outlives the iteration.

The receiver must certainly be a builtin `list`: a list display or comprehension, `list(...)`,
or a `list[...]` / `List[...]` annotation on a parameter, a local, or a class attribute
(`self.items`). Calls on a `set`, a `str`, a project class, or a receiver of unknown type are
not reported. Neither are:

- loops whose size does not depend on the data: small constant ranges and displays
  (`for i in range(3)`, `for s in SUFFIXES` with `SUFFIXES = (".py", ".pyi")`, also through
  `enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()` and `range(ATTEMPTS - 1)` with a
  constant `ATTEMPTS`), retry loops, and daemon polling loops; the iterable of a `for` loop,
  which runs once;
- lists built in the iteration (`parts = [...]` inside the loop) and lists of the loop element
  (`row.cells.index(x)`);
- small lists: a display of at most 8 items that nothing grows (the loop may shrink it with
  `remove()` / `pop()` or replace its items), in the function, as a module global (also of
  another module: `LEVELS = ["low", "mid", "high"]`), or as an attribute its class and
  subclasses only ever assign such a display (`self.preferred = [",", ";"]`, a class
  attribute). A display handed to code that may grow it (any call but read-only builtins; a
  `*items` argument passes the items only) is not small;
- calls after which the loop always ends (`return items.index(x)`, a `break` on every path);
- `index(x, start)`, which scans from a position that usually moves forward.

## Why is this bad?
Each call scans the list from the start (and `remove()` also shifts the elements after the
removed one), so the loop costs the product of the loop size and the list size: O(n²) when both
grow with the input. A `dict` or `set` built once before the loop answers each lookup in
constant time, and `collections.Counter` counts every value in one pass.

## Example
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    return [names.index(w) for w in winners]


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    for x in unwanted:
        items.remove(x)
```

Use instead:
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    position = {}
    for i, name in enumerate(names):
        position.setdefault(name, i)  # the first index, as `list.index`
    return [position[w] for w in winners]  # `KeyError` where `index` raised `ValueError`


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    gone = set(unwanted)
    items[:] = [x for x in items if x not in gone]
```

The rewrites are not drop-in replacements: `remove()` drops only the first occurrence of each
value and raises `ValueError` for a missing one, and the values must be hashable.

The advice follows what the loop does with the list. Removals can wait for one rebuild after
the loop only when the loop reads the list nowhere else (a membership test guarding the removal,
`if x in items: items.remove(x)`, aside); when it iterates, tests, indexes, or passes on the list
after a removal (a greedy match over the remaining values), the message advises a `set` or a
`dict` with constant-time deletion instead. An index or a count built once before the loop stays
right only while the loop does not change the list, in place or through a project function it
hands the list to (`change(names)` where `change` calls `names.reverse()`); otherwise the
message advises keeping it up to date with each change.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/

# loop-linear-membership (OPT110)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop.

## What it does
Checks membership tests against a list or tuple inside a loop, `e in lst`, where the list does
not change during the loop, and suggests building a `set` once before the loop.

This is a size-dependent rewrite: it is reported as a suggestion and applied only with
`heki check --fix --include-size-dependent`, or for functions that a `--profile` dump shows
hot. Not reported:

- small displays: at most 8 items that nothing grows, whatever the items are
  (`x in ("a", "b")`, `x in [b"1", b"2"]`, also through a name bound to one);
- lists whose elements are dicts, lists, or sets: no `set` can hold them.

## Why is this bad?
`e in lst` scans the list, so the loop costs the product of both sizes. A set lookup is
constant time once the set exists.

## Example
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = list(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

Use instead:
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = set(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when:

- the container is an exact `list` / `tuple` bound outside the loop and not changed inside it
  (a list mutated in the loop would make the hoisted set stale);
- every element is an `int`, `str`, `bytes`, `bool`, or `float`: building the set cannot raise
  even when the loop runs zero times, and hashing agrees with `==`;
- the probe value is of those types too (an object with a custom `__eq__` could match list
  elements a set lookup never compares with).

A `list[int]` annotation is never trusted: a list subclass can override `__contains__`.

Not reported when the container is a small display that nothing grows, or when the loop runs a
fixed small number of times (`for i in range(3):`): building the set costs about as much as the
scans it saves.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/

# loop-unpooled-client (EFF102)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Allocating an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or sessionless request inside a loop.

## What it does
Checks loops that allocate a network or database client on every iteration: module-level
request helpers that open a new connection per call (`requests.get`, `httpx.get`), client
constructors, sync and async (`requests.Session()`, `httpx.AsyncClient()`,
`aiohttp.ClientSession()`, `boto3.client(...)`), connection factories (`sqlite3.connect`,
`redis.Redis`, `create_async_engine`, ...), and connection pools (`psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool`),
directly or through project functions,
including the getter of a property read in the loop (`self.client.get(url)` where the `client`
getter builds a new client).

The iterable of a `for` loop is evaluated once and is not reported; neither are calls in
loops whose size the code fixes, when no data-sized loop is around them: displays of at most 8
items (also through a name or a module constant bound to one that nothing grows, and through
`enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()`), `range` of integer constants
(`range(ATTEMPTS - 1)`), retry loops, and daemon polling loops.

A client that is only created while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets (lazy
initialization: `if not self._sock: self._sock = connect()`, or `if self._sock: return`
before connecting), is created once per object, not on every iteration: the call is not
reported unless a data-sized loop around it constructs the object in each iteration
(`Connection().send(cmd)`); `conn.send(cmd)` on a connection made before the loop, taken from
a pool, or held by the receiver is not reported.

A call whose arguments switch off the branch that creates the client is not followed into
it: `load(name, cache=False)` does not reach the `urlopen` under `if cache:` in `load`. This
covers constant arguments and the literal defaults of omitted ones (`False`, `None`, `0`, `""`,
empty displays), tests the caller has already made on the same value (`isinstance`, `is None`,
truthiness), and wrappers that pass the value on.

## Why is this bad?
Each new client pays for DNS, TCP, and TLS setup again and throws its connection pool away.
In a loop this dominates the run time and exhausts sockets.

## Example
```python
import requests


def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for url in urls:
        out.append(requests.get(url).text)  # EFF102: a new connection per iteration
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    with requests.Session() as session:
        return [session.get(url).text for url in urls]
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/

# nested-loop-equijoin (OPT113)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index.

## What it does
Checks nested loops that join two collections by comparing a key of each with `==`:
`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k:`, including a comprehension as the inner loop
(`[b for b in B if b.k == a.k]`).

The keys are the loop elements themselves, their unpacked components (`for k, v in pairs`),
attributes (`a.k`, `a.x.y`), and constant subscripts (`a["k"]`, `a[0]`). Both loops must be
`for` loops whose size depends on the data. The rule reports one diagnostic per inner loop, at
its first matching comparison. It does not report:

- traversals, where the inner iterable is computed from the outer element
  (`for b in a.children`, `for b in index[a.k]`, `for b in f(a)`, `for b in xs[i + 1:]`);
- comparisons that do not select pairs: `!=`, a negated `==`, one alternative of an `or`
  (`a.k == b.k or match(a, b)`), a result that is stored instead of tested, a value picked for
  every pair (`1 if a.k == b.k else 0`), a match that only skips to the next iteration
  (`if a == b: continue` in an all-pairs loop), or a comparison whose false side does work:
  an `else` / `elif` body, the failure of an `assert a == b`, a `break` / `return` on a
  mismatch, or statements that only the mismatches run because a match `break`s. They run for
  the pairs an index would skip, so every pair is needed; statements after the `if` that every
  pair runs do not count;
- loops whose size the code fixes: a display of at most 8 items (`for b in ("x", "y")`, also
  through a name or a module constant bound to one that nothing grows, and through
  `enumerate` / `zip` / `sorted` / `.items()` ...), and `range` of integer constants.

## Why is this bad?
The inner loop runs completely for every outer element, so the join costs O(n·m) comparisons.
Indexing the inner collection by its key once (a `dict` from key to elements, or a `set` of the
keys) makes it O(n + m). A `break` after the first match does not help much: a missing key
still scans the whole inner collection.

## Example
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    for order in orders:
        for customer in customers:
            if order.customer_id == customer.id:
                order.customer = customer
                break
```

Use instead:
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    by_id = {}
    for customer in customers:
        by_id.setdefault(customer.id, customer)  # the first match, as the `break`
    for order in orders:
        customer = by_id.get(order.customer_id)
        if customer is not None:
            order.customer = customer
```

The advice follows how the matches are used. When a match leaves the inner loop (`break`,
`return`, `raise`), one element per key is enough: a `set` of the elements, or a `dict` from the
key to its first element, as above. When every match is used (`out.append((a, b))` for each
equal pair), a `set` or a one-element `dict` would drop the repeated matches, so the message
advises a `dict` from each key (or value) to the list of its elements.

The keys must be hashable, and `==` must agree with their hash. When a key is known to be a
`list`, `dict`, `set`, or `bytearray` (from its annotation, or as an element of a display of
such displays), the message advises indexing a hashable form of it instead (a `tuple` or
`frozenset` of its items).

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/

# read-owner-violation (MUT203)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`.

## What it does
Checks reads of attributes that a `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of
allowed reader functions: the read side of `MUT201`. A read is reported when it happens outside
the allowed readers:

- directly (`ref.children`), also on `self` and through local aliases;
- through `getattr(ref, "children"[, default])` or `object.__getattribute__(ref, "children")`
  with a constant name: a string literal or a module-level `Final` string constant;
- through `ref.__dict__["children"]` or `ref.__dict__.get("children")`, also with a `Final`
  constant for the key.

A target names a class and an attribute; it covers the class's subclasses too. A container
entry (`Class.attr["key"]`) is a write target only: reading an entry reads the attribute, so a
read target names `Class.attr` (an entry is a configuration error).

The read object's class is the one heki infers for it, with annotations as hints: a
parameter, local, attribute, or return annotation, including the items of `list[...]`,
`Sequence[...]`, `Iterable[...]`, `Iterator[...]`, `Generator[...]`, `dict[...]`,
`Mapping[...]`, `tuple[...]`, and `set[...]`; a constructor call; and what the object comes
from: a loop over such a container (`for model in models`), a subscript (`models[0]`,
`by_name["a"]`), unpacking (`model, _ = pair`), `dict` views and `get` / `pop`, `enumerate`,
`zip`, `reversed`, `sorted`, `iter`, `next`, `list` / `tuple` / `set`, `itertools.chain`, a
display, the items appended to a local list, or a comprehension or generator expression. A
method call or a `@property` / `cached_property` read has the return annotation of the
definition the receiver's class finds first along its MRO, as for a type checker (`typing.Self`
is the receiver's class); a copy (`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`,
`model_copy`) has its original's class, calling a `functools.partial` object returns what the
wrapped function returns, and `typing.cast` names the class. A variable rebound in a loop
(`node = node.parent`) or assigned on some paths only (a walrus inside `and` / `or`) has the
classes of the values reaching it; a value of two or three classes (`Model | Node`, from an
annotation or from different assignments) is each of them, and an `isinstance` check narrows it
in the code it guards (`if isinstance(x, Model): ...`, `if not isinstance(x, Model): return`,
also inside `and` / `or`). A value typed with a project `Protocol` is an instance of the project
classes that implement it structurally (having every member it defines; at most eight, counting
a class and not its subclasses). An object whose class heki cannot see (an unannotated parameter
or return, `Any`, a value of more than three classes) is not tied to the target.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with
project callers hands the responsibility to its callers: the read is reported at every call
site of the first non-private callers above it, with the chain of calls as related
information. Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute calls its getter,
so a private getter (`ref._kids` returning `self.children`) hands its read to the functions
reading it. Reads in a class's own initializer on its own `self` are allowed, and so are reads
in a function that only runs inside allowed contexts (every path of callers above it starts in
an allowed reader or an exempt method), as for `MUT201`. One report stands for every read behind
its call (`sites` in JSON), as for `MUT201`. A read runs where the body holding it runs, as for
`MUT201`: a generator's reads where it is iterated, a coroutine's where it is awaited.

## Why is this bad?
Some state is only meaningful through the component that maintains it: an index that keeps a
derived view consistent, a store that resolves references lazily. Reading the raw attribute
elsewhere sees stale or partial data, and the bug only shows up for some inputs. The contract
states which functions may read it once in configuration, with no runtime cost.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*"]
message = "read children through GenerationIndex instead"
```

```python
class Reference:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.children: list["Reference"] = []


class GenerationIndex:
    def children_of(self, ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
        return list(ref.children)  # allowed reader


def _kids(ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
    return ref.children


def render(ref: Reference) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, _kids(ref)))  # MUT203: reads `Reference.children` via `_kids`
```

Use instead:
```python
def render(ref: Reference, index: GenerationIndex) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, index.children_of(ref)))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: `Class.attr` entries; globs and dotted suffixes match.
  - `allowed-readers`: functions allowed to read the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname.
  - `forbidden-readers`: when set, only reads by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-readers`; `forbidden-readers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not read the
    targets); `allowed-readers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A read is in
    scope when the reporting function or a private helper it hands the read through is
    forbidden.
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to read the targets (`__repr__`, `__deepcopy__`); a plain
    name matches any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched
    like `allowed-readers`.
  - `message`: appended to every message of the contract.

Known limitation: a read through a parameter without a project-class annotation
(`def helper(ref): return ref.children`) is not seen, since the read object's class is unknown
there; unlike a write, a read is not handed to the caller that knows it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/

# readonly-param-mutation (MUT110)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Enabled by default · No automatic fix

Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameter to a function that changes it in place (directly, through an alias, or through helpers).

## What it does
Checks functions that hand a parameter annotated as a read-only container to code that changes
